scenes.vo: UT San Antonio says some people could have ankle-deep water in their yard before a flood warning sounds on their phone.
scenes.on_screen: A disclosed design detail with no yard around it: brown water climbs over the lowest optical lens at ankle height and the lens lights as it goes under. On the same ankle height the picture cuts to a San Antonio yard with no station in it, the water spreading past the orange ankle mark on a chain link post as the view pulls back. The water keeps rising to the rain boots on the porch step while the phone on the porch rail stays dark. The flash flood warning banner finally slides onto the phone, after the water is already in the yard.

scenes.vo: When the risk rises, a radio signal can carry more than a half-mile through city streets, and up to five miles in open country, to a hub.
scenes.on_screen: From above, amber rings leave the station dot on the street map, the half-mile and five-mile labels appearing as each circle is reached. At street level the rings run down the street of bungalows and pass the half-mile tag on the far corner post. Across open country the leading ring reaches the hub's rooftop mast, its lamp lights as the ring arrives and the five-mile tag pins.

requests.purpose: Carry one solar flood station through the film so the viewer follows its sun-charged battery, its four optical marks lighting as the water crosses them, the chip that lights an amber risk lamp on the spot and the antenna that sends the radio pulse, with every state it reaches kept for the rest of the film.
requests.prompt: Author an original finished React and SVG object in the current Remotion engine. A weathered galvanized steel post set beside a San Antonio street with a lopsided, slightly tilted instrument housing, a small dark blue solar panel with a worn corner, a short whip antenna, a battery bar window, and a column of four optical water-level marks mounted at four different heights, each with a small lens and a lamp. A cutaway view shows a small chip with thin traces and one amber risk lamp, with no logos and no real hardware brand. Late afternoon storm light from the upper left, cool sky fill, a long soft shadow, a rust drip and a dent, nothing symmetric. A disclosed illustration of the described design, never an installed unit.
requests.source_limit: Disclosed illustration of the design the University of Texas at San Antonio describes. Not an installed station, a real street, a measured water level or a real result.

requests.purpose: Give the station a believable world: the San Antonio street and yard where water rises, the porch phone, the radio rings, the hub building, the hub dashboard map and the empty map.
requests.prompt: Author an original finished React and SVG support group in the current Remotion engine. A wet San Antonio residential street with a chain link fence post, a limestone curb, a live oak edge and a porch rail with a worn phone, brown flood water with a hand drawn edge, a small hub building with a rooftop mast, a hub desk with a monitor and a sleeved forearm, a flat dashboard map of streets with shaded flood paths and outlined risk zones, an empty map card with no pin, and thin radio rings with a half-mile tag and a five-mile tag. Maintained but worn, nothing symmetric, warm limestone and storm gray palette, no real brand marks. A disclosed illustration.
requests.source_limit: Disclosed illustration. Not a real San Antonio address, hub, dashboard, responder or deployment. The university names no installation site.

film_direction.angle: The viewer starts on a disclosed design detail, the lowest optical lens going under at ankle height, then cuts on that height to a flooded yard with no station in it and the late phone.
film_direction.opening_promise: Watch four sensor marks get wet and see what a self-powered station does with that.
film_direction.performed_turn: The chip lights a local risk judgment with no line to a server, then a radio pulse carries it to a hub.
film_direction.closing_answer: The design says yes, a station can judge a flooding street on its own power. The proof so far is validation accuracy, and the university names no place that has installed one.

clauses.text: UT San Antonio says some people could have ankle-deep water in their yard before a flood warning sounds on their phone.
So its researchers built a flood station that charges itself from light and needs no cell tower.
Four optical sensors at different heights watch the water, along with rain, temperature, humidity and light.
A small chip on the station runs the AI itself, so it judges flood risk without a central server.
When the risk rises, a radio signal can carry more than a half-mile through city streets, and up to five miles in open country, to a hub.
At the hub, a second, larger AI model draws a map of how flooding could spread, for emergency responders.
The university reports ninety eight point eight two percent validation accuracy from early assessments after training, and no field result.
It names no town that has installed one.

story_contract.opening_question: Can a flood station judge rising street water with no power line and no cell tower?

story_contract.action: Built a prototype flood station that charges itself from light and runs its AI model on a small chip.

story_contract.closing_answer: The design says yes. The proof so far is validation accuracy, and no installed place is named.

scenes.advances: A disclosed design detail with no yard around it: brown water climbs over the lowest optical lens at ankle height and the lens lights as it goes under. On the same ankle height the picture cuts to a San Antonio yard with no station in it, the water spreading past the orange ankle mark on a chain link post as the view pulls back. The water keeps rising to the rain boots on the porch step while the phone on the porch rail stays dark. The flash flood warning banner finally slides onto the phone, after the water is already in the yard.

The view cranes down from the antenna tip and reveals the whole prototype flood station at a curb, and a prototype tag pins. Low sun reaches the small dark solar panel, a glint crosses its cells and the battery bar fills cell by cell. A dashed line leaves the antenna toward a far cell tower and stops halfway, and a no cell tower needed tag pins.

Four optical lenses at four different heights on the post catch the low light in turn. Brown water rises past the lit first lens and reaches the second, which lights as it goes under. Rain, temperature, humidity and light lamps come on one by one on the housing, each with its label.

Seen from the street through the housing window, readings run along the thin traces to the small chip. The chip lights the amber risk lamp on the board and a judged on the station tag pins. Far from the station a dashed outline of a central server draws itself and stays dark, with no line running to it.

From above, amber rings leave the station dot on the street map, the half-mile and five-mile labels appearing as each circle is reached. At street level the rings run down the street of bungalows and pass the half-mile tag on the far corner post. Across open country the leading ring reaches the hub's rooftop mast, its lamp lights as the ring arrives and the five-mile tag pins.

On the hub's screen, dots from several stations arrive and a tag names the second, larger model. Shaded flood paths spread out from the first dots along the creek and the low streets. At the desk the dashed higher-risk outlines settle on the screen, a responder's sleeved forearm comes to rest beside it and a for emergency responders tag pins.

hero.silhouette: A tall galvanized post with a tilted boxy housing, a small dark solar panel, a whip antenna and a column of four lens marks at four different heights.
hero.finish: Lit upper-left steel edges, cool shaded right side, a rust drip, a dent in the housing cap, a worn panel corner, small lens glints, a chip cutaway with thin traces and a long soft ground shadow.

art_direction.motion_language: Water rises at an even speed and marks light as it crosses them, radio rings expand and fade, cards and tags settle without bounce, and the camera holds while objects perform, moving only to follow the water or to pull back.
